Overview

At Roundforest, we run high-volume Google traffic campaigns sending millions of global shoppers to data-driven "Top 10" product review lists. The platform earns a commission from Amazon on every purchase triggered by a user clickout - meaning even tiny friction points in the journey translate into massive revenue impact.

Problem

Millions of high-intent shoppers were dropping off before clicking through to buy.

At Roundforest, we run high-volume Google traffic campaigns sending millions of global shoppers to data-driven "Top 10" product review lists. The platform earns a commission from Amazon on every purchase triggered by a user clickout - meaning even tiny friction points in the journey translate into massive revenue impact.

We observed two core issues: users were moving through content quickly with low meaningful engagement, and the experience lacked clear guidance for fast, confident decision-making - especially on mobile. We also needed more reliable short-cycle UX signals to support rapid experimentation.

Millions
Global shoppers reached monthly via paid Google traffic
Low
Meaningful engagement despite high purchase intent on arrival
3 Phases

Strategy & Approach

I led an experimentation-driven UX process focused on improving early behavioral signals and reducing decision friction. Instead of large redesigns, I broke the experience into small, testable hypotheses around intent capture, clarity, and scanability. Each iteration was validated through A/B testing, with a focus on interaction quality and decision-flow improvements.

Design Process
Observe → Hypothesize → Test → Iterate
Observe
Funnel analysis, behavioral data, and engagement metrics to surface friction points.
Hypothesize
Break problems into small, testable UX hypotheses around intent, clarity, and scanability.
Design & Test
A/B test variants with live traffic - validate interaction quality over assumptions.
Iterate
Compound wins from each validated iteration - reject what hurts, scale what works.
Hands-On Design process
Three phases of funnel transformation

Each phase targeted a specific funnel stage - from intent capture to final clickout decision.

Phase 01 · Mid-Funnel Intent Capture
"Narrow Down" Interactive Filter Funnel

Introduced interactive tag chips letting users instantly segment product lists - eliminating choice paralysis for high-intent, low-patience traffic. Three A/B iterations refined copy, visual prominence, layout behavior, and a contextual default state to guide users and signal interactivity.

1st Iteration
Tweaking for Better Engagement

We noticed a really positive trend in clickouts and EPU (earnings per user), but the overall engagement with the feature itself wasn't quite where we wanted it. To fix that, we ran another iteration focusing on the UI and messaging—making it more visually appealing and enticing for sellers to actually click on and try out.

2nd Iteration
↕ Scroll inside the screens
Phase 02 · Bottom-Funnel Conversion Push
Mobile Product Page Redesign

Redesigned the mobile product page to reduce cognitive load and improve final clickout decisions - keeping UI continuity with the list page for a seamless, low-friction flow.

Balancing Engagement & Conversions
  • Protecting Core Revenue: Only highly engaged users were funneled to the new page, so we kept the "Read Full Review" button subtle.
  • Familiarity Above the Fold: The primary CTA stayed above the fold, with UI matched to the "Top 10 List" page for familiarity.
  • A Lean Feedback Loop: A lean "Didn't Match" link catches feedback without distracting from the main goal.
Phase 3 · Experiment
Phase 03 · Feature-Rich Layout Experiment
More Information, Less Conversion

Tested a more feature-dense mobile product card with additional specs and interactive elements. The hypothesis: richer information would support more confident decision-making. High contrast, clear borders, and strong element separation were designed for accessibility and readability. The experiment negatively impacted clickout behavior - increased density disrupted page hierarchy and added friction for fast-scanning mobile traffic.

Designing for Our Audience

Looking at the data, I noticed a huge chunk of our users were aged 55+. This insight directly shaped several key design choices to ensure better accessibility and engagement:

  • Boosting Accessibility: I maximized visual contrast and made clickable elements significantly larger to ensure everything was easy to see and tap.
  • Cleaner Visuals: I used crisp, clear strokes and cut down on the color palette to reduce visual noise.
  • Driving Curiosity: We placed clear, inviting interactive elements throughout the flow to spark curiosity and naturally boost engagement.
✕ Test failed, did not scale
Key Takeaways
What this taught us
Design for proxy signals. In fast-moving e-commerce, optimizing upstream behaviors like engagement and readability is the most reliable way to improve downstream conversion outcomes.
Friction compounds at scale. Small UX improvements become significant when applied across large traffic volumes - each iteration's gains stack across millions of sessions.
Mobile requires intentional simplification. Effective mobile UX prioritizes clarity, reduced density, and interaction patterns that support quick scanning and confident decision-making.
